title: Data representation
body:
Everything in [[Main memory]] is bits. "Data representation" is the set of agreements about
what a given run of bits means, because the bits themselves carry no type. The same 8 bits
`01000001` are the number 65, the character `A`, or part of an instruction, depending only
on what the program does with them.

This is the thing [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTER SCIENCE 2]] hid behind [[Data type]]. In C the
compiler remembers that a variable is an `int` and stops you from misusing it. In
[[Assembly]] nothing remembers: you pick `.b`, `.w`, or `.l` and you are responsible for the
interpretation. A [[Type casting|cast]] in C is exactly this, telling the compiler to change
its mind about bits that did not move.

The four representations the course cares about:

| Kind | Note | Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Integers | [[Integer Representation]] | binary, two's [[Complements\|complement]] for negatives |
| Characters | [[Character Representation]] | [[ASCII]], 7 bits in a [[Byte]] |
| Booleans | [[Boolean Representation]] | zero is false, non-zero is true |
| Instructions | [[Instructions]] | opcode plus operand fields, also just bits |

Writing the same value in a different base ([[Base Conversion]]) does not change the
representation, only how you as a human wrote it down. `$41`, `%01000001`, `@101`, and `65`
are one byte.
